modules.title: How Data Is Actually Stored
modules.description: Every lesson in this course after Level 1 reads data — SELECT, WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY. None of them explain how the data got there or how tables relate to each other, and a learner who can only read cannot build a database to practise on. This module fixes both, using named chapters of the same freeCodeCamp course you already opened in lesson 1.

lessons.title: Tables, Keys and How Data Relates
lessons.description: What a table actually is, and how primary and foreign keys connect one table to another — the idea that makes JOINs make sense later.
objectives: Describe a table in terms of rows, columns and data types
Explain what a primary key is and why every table needs one
Explain how a foreign key links one table to another
lessons.notes:
WATCH THE **"Tables & Keys"** CHAPTER of this course — navigate by the chapter name in the video's description, not by a timestamp someone quoted. This is the same 4-hour freeCodeCamp course you opened in lesson 1, so it should already be in your history; you are watching a different twenty minutes of it, not downloading it again. That matters when data costs money.

The idea to hold onto: a table is one kind of thing — one table for customers, one for orders, never both mixed together. A PRIMARY KEY is the column that makes each row uniquely identifiable, so that "customer 4051" always means exactly one person. A FOREIGN KEY is a column in one table that holds another table's primary key, and that is the entire mechanism by which an order knows which customer it belongs to.

This is why the JOIN lesson in Level 2 works. A JOIN is not magic — it follows a foreign key back to the primary key it points at. Learners who find JOINs confusing almost always never learned keys, and the fix is this chapter rather than more JOIN practice.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — the course uses MySQL, and so does most of the job market's entry-level SQL work. The concepts here are identical in PostgreSQL, SQL Server, SQLite and the Postgres database behind Supabase; only some function names and installation steps differ. Do not worry that you picked the wrong one. Nobody who can explain keys is turned away for having learned them in MySQL.
lessons.practice: On paper, design two tables for a small business you know — say a shop's customers and its orders. Write out the column names and mark the primary key in each. Then draw the arrow: which column in the orders table points at which column in the customers table? Finally, write one sentence explaining what would go wrong if the orders table just stored the customer's name as text instead.

quiz.question: What is a primary key for?
options: It makes each row uniquely identifiable, so a given id always means exactly one record
It limits how many rows a table can hold

quiz.question: Why do learners who find JOINs confusing usually need this chapter rather than more JOIN practice?
options: A JOIN follows a foreign key back to the primary key it points at, so without keys the operation has no meaning
JOINs only work on tables created in the same session

lessons.title: Making Your Own Database to Practise On
lessons.description: Creating tables and putting rows into them — so you have data of your own to query instead of only reading someone else's examples.
objectives: Create a table with appropriate columns and data types
Insert rows into a table you made
Explain why practising on your own data beats following along with a sample database
lessons.notes:
WATCH TWO CHAPTERS, in order: **"Creating Tables"**, then **"Inserting Data"**. Same video as the previous lesson — again, navigate by chapter name.

This is the single biggest hole in this course as it stands. Everything else here reads data that already exists. If you cannot create a table and put rows in it, you can only ever follow along with somebody else's example database, and following along is not the same as knowing how.

CREATE TABLE names the columns and says what kind of data each one holds — text, number, date. INSERT puts rows in. That is genuinely all you need to make a practice database, and once you have one, every other lesson in this course becomes something you can try on data you understand rather than a demo you watch.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — what to build first, and a warning. Build the two tables you designed on paper in the previous lesson, with about ten rows each, using real-ish data from something you know: a shop, a chama's contributions, a class register. Ten rows is enough to see a JOIN work and small enough to check by eye whether the answer is right — which is the actual skill, because SQL will happily return a confidently wrong answer to a badly written query.

The warning: practise on a database you created, never on a live one belonging to anyone else. DELETE and UPDATE without a WHERE clause will remove or overwrite every row in the table, instantly, with no undo. That mistake has ended jobs. Level 2 covers WHERE; until you are fluent with it, keep your experiments in your own practice database.
lessons.practice: Create the two tables you designed on paper and insert about ten rows into each, using data you actually recognise. Then run a SELECT on each table and check the output against what you typed. Finally, deliberately break something small — insert a row whose foreign key points at a customer that does not exist — and see what the database does about it. What it refuses to do is as informative as what it allows.

quiz.question: Why is being able to CREATE and INSERT the biggest gap in a read-only SQL course?
options: Employers test CREATE TABLE more often than SELECT
Without it you can only follow along with someone else's example database, and following along is not the same as knowing how
SELECT does not work on tables you did not create
It is required before you can install MySQL

quiz.question: Why practise only on a database you created yourself?
options: Live databases run too slowly for practice
DELETE or UPDATE without a WHERE clause wipes or overwrites every row instantly, with no undo
Your own database returns results faster
